justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across time horizons, starting near 43.1 at the one-day mark and gradually rising to 44.0 at the one-month horizon. The one-day estimate was anchored primarily by recent price action, momentum indicators, and the assumption that no major macro surprises would materialize within the next session. Markets tend to exhibit short-term mean reversion around recent levels, so the estimate stayed close to the last observed price. The one-week and one-month estimates incorporate a slight positive drift, consistent with a modestly bullish underlying trend — perhaps reflecting expectations of continued economic resilience, stable interest rate expectations, or sector-specific tailwinds. The drift is intentionally small because strong directional conviction at these horizons is rarely warranted without a clear catalyst.

Confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, going from a relatively tight 3.2-point spread at one day to a much broader 11-point spread at one month. This reflects the compounding of uncertainty over time — even if daily volatility is modest, uncertainty accumulates and the range of plausible outcomes grows nonlinearly. At the one-day horizon, the dominant sources of uncertainty are intraday liquidity conditions, any scheduled economic releases, and short-term order flow dynamics. At the one-week level, macro data prints, central bank communications, and sentiment shifts become more meaningful contributors. At one month, earnings announcements, geopolitical developments, and broader market regime changes all enter the picture and can move prices materially in either direction.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, a surprise deterioration in inflation data or an unexpected hawkish turn from a major central bank could trigger a sharp risk-off move, potentially pushing prices well below the lower bounds. A sudden geopolitical escalation or credit event in a systemically important institution could have a similar effect. On the upside, a blowout earnings report, an unexpectedly dovish policy signal, or a short-squeeze in heavily shorted positions could propel prices above the upper confidence bounds. These tail events, by definition, are assigned low probability but are not negligible, and the 90% intervals I provided are designed to exclude roughly 10% of outcomes that reflect exactly these kinds of surprises.
